text: Anna Catharina Bischoff (23 March 1719 – 30 August 1787), known as the "Lady (or mummy) of the Barfüsser Church," was the wife of pastor Lucas Gernler. Her mummified body was discovered in 1975 in a shaft at the Barfüsser Church in Basel, Switzerland, during a renovation that involved the excavation and documentation of hundreds of burial sites by the city's archaeological department. On 20 October 1975, workers found a brick-walled grave chamber in front of the choir containing two well-preserved coffins on a pile of bones: the upper coffin held a female skeleton, and the smaller one beneath contained a completely mummified woman, later identified as Anna Catharina Bischoff. She was buried in a simple spruce wood coffin, with her left hand holding her right arm above the wrist; her body was mostly intact, with only the head and feet decomposed, and parts of her dress and hair preserved. She stood 142 cm tall with a stout build. In 1976, anthropologist Bruno Kaufmann found mercury sulfide throughout her body—especially in the lungs—responsible for the mummification, with atmospheric conditions in the coffin and chamber preventing microbial decay. Since 2015, the mummy has been studied at the Natural History Museum of Basel using computer tomography, which revealed atherosclerosis in the abdominal aorta and gallstones, indicating a diet rich in carbohydrates and fatty meat. She had lost all her upper jaw teeth due to a sugary diet and poor oral hygiene, though her lower incisors and canines remained preserved. The presence of mercury in her lungs and organs led medical historians in the 1970s to conclude she had undergone mercury inhalation therapy, a common treatment for severe syphilis at the time. However, modern analysis shows the mercury level was below the threshold for poisoning, so it cannot be confirmed whether it caused her death; further investigation is needed to determine if syphilis or a combination of syphilis and mercury exposure led to her death. Her grave's prominent location suggests she belonged to a privileged class, reserved for high clergy or dignitaries. Church records indicate that the shaft had been opened before 1843 during a renovation when the nave was converted into a commercial warehouse; when workers removed memorial slab number 11, they found a grave with three coffins. In 2016, Marie-Louise Gamma and Diana Gysin, citizen-researchers from Basel, discovered in contractor Blendinger’s notes that slab 11 contained the remains of Isaak Byschoff, a former Hospital Master, who died in 1709, and his wife Catharina Gyssendorfferin, who died in 1697. The record notes that Anna Catharina Bischoff, the granddaughter of Isaak Bischoff, was buried in August 1787. Blendinger described a walled grave with two black and one yellow coffin, all well-preserved, with the yellow one containing a small female corpse resembling a mummy, which matched the 1975 mummy. A research team from Eurac Research in Bozen isolated mitochondrial DNA from the mummy, identifying a haplogroup U variant, enabling scientific identification. Genealogists from Basel’s citizen-researchers reconstructed a continuous female lineage from Justina Froben (born 1512), daughter of printer Johann Froben, through 15 generations to Rosemary Probst-Ryhiner, and found a second line in the US. DNA analysis of both families showed over 99.8% similarity to the mummy’s DNA, confirming Anna Catharina Bischoff’s identity and burial date. A direct lineage through her son-in-law Christian Friedrich Pfeffel von Kriegelstein connects to British politician Boris Johnson, whose great-grandmother was Marie Luise von Pfeffel. A BBC team reported on this connection in January 2018 at a media event in Basel’s Natural History Museum. Anna Catharina was the eldest of five siblings, born in Strasbourg to reformed pastor Johann Jakob Bischoff (1683–1733) and Augusta Margaretha Burckhardt (1697–1735); her father died when she was 14, and her mother returned to Basel with her daughters. Before moving, Anna Catharina met Lucas Gernler (1704–1781), 15 years her senior, who served as a substitute pastor in Wolfisheim in 1732/33 and later succeeded her father. After marrying in 1738, they returned to Strasbourg, where Anna Catharina had seven children, only two of whom survived childhood. Her daughter Anna Katharina Gernler (1739–1776) married Christian Friedrich Pfeffel von Kriegelstein and died in Versailles in 1776. Lucas Gernler died in 1781 from a stroke at age 77, and Anna Catharina moved to Basel the following year at age 62. She likely lived with her younger sister Anna Margareta Geymüller-Bischoff (1724–1804), who married a wealthy trader. Her great-grandson Karl Maximilian von Pfeffel (1811–1890) married Karoline von Rothenburg, the illegitimate daughter of Prince Paul of Württemberg, making Boris Johnson a seventh-generation descendant. A team of 40 experts from anthropology, genealogy, forensic medicine, molecular biology, history of medicine, and toxicology conducted the research, though several questions remain open. The team continues to investigate these questions and aims to publish a book on Anna Catharina Bischoff’s life and work, in collaboration with the University of Basel’s History Department and coordinated at the Basel Museum of Natural History.
